article_title: Effects of a Generative AI Virtual Patient on Serious Illness Communication Skills: Randomized Controlled Trial.
citation: Haut KG, Hasan M, Carroll T, Epstein RM, Sen T, Hoque E. (2026). Effects of a Generative AI Virtual Patient on Serious Illness Communication Skills: Randomized Controlled Trial. JMIR Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.2196/93034
title: MVP framework and 3E communication skills for serious illness conversations
description: The MVP (medical situation, values, and plan) communication framework and its 3 core skills—Empathize, Be Explicit, and Empower (3Es)—ground both the SOPHIE system and the study's outcome measures. The Empathize skill focuses on responding to emotional distress, Be Explicit on clearly communicating prognosis and uncertainty, and Empower on eliciting values and supporting a patient-centered care plan. The framework was converted into a structured Likert-scale questionnaire to quantify communication behaviors on a numeric scale, normalized to between 0 and 1.
requirements: Raters must be trained on the rubric to produce consistent scores
constraints: The rubric was intended to capture within-participant improvement from before to after the intervention, not to define an ideal level of performance or estimate population-level clinical competence
target_learners: Medical, nursing, and physician assistant students
target_learning_goals: Serious illness communication skills (Empathize, Be Explicit, Empower)
examples: Used as the primary outcome framework: SPs and 4 blinded raters evaluated participants pre- and postintervention using a rubric based on this framework
key_sources: Haut KG, Hasan M, Carroll T, Epstein RM, Sen T, Hoque E. (2026). Effects of a Generative AI Virtual Patient on Serious Illness Communication Skills: Randomized Controlled Trial. JMIR Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.2196/93034

article_title: Impact of a Competency-based Mechanical Ventilation Course Using Virtual Simulation.
citation: Rocha de Macedo Bruno, Lima Carolina Saldanha, Haydar Ahmed, Holanda Marcelo Alcantara, Hayashi Fatima Kiyoko, Ferreira Juliana Carvalho. (2025). Impact of a Competency-based Mechanical Ventilation Course Using Virtual Simulation. ATS Scholar. https://doi.org/10.34197/ats-scholar.2024-0083OC
title: Online competency-based mechanical ventilation course with virtual simulation (Xlung) for internal medicine residents
description: An 8-month online competency-based MV course built on 20 competencies adapted from a recommended MV competency guideline, organized into eight modules. Six modules combined a 1-hour live online meeting — "20 minutes of didactic lecture and 40 minutes for training using a virtual web-based simulator platform (Xlung)" — with self-directed learning material, retention quizzes, and Google Classroom delivery; two modules were exclusively self-directed. Engagement was reinforced through live meetings, an online platform, and group chats, and all residents received 1 month of deliberate simulator practice before the virtual SBA.
requirements: Access to the Xlung virtual simulator platform and Google Classroom
Live sessions limited to 1 hour, scheduled in the early evening to respect duty hours
constraints: Developed and delivered during the COVID-19 pandemic with all activities online
Two modules were exclusively self-directed without live simulation
target_learners: Internal medicine residents in a large university hospital residency program
target_learning_goals: Applying mechanical ventilation knowledge to simulated ICU scenarios across 20 MV competencies
examples: 81 of 103 residents completed the course, rating it effective with a net promoter score of 9.2
key_sources: Rocha de Macedo Bruno, Lima Carolina Saldanha, Haydar Ahmed, Holanda Marcelo Alcantara, Hayashi Fatima Kiyoko, Ferreira Juliana Carvalho. (2025). Impact of a Competency-based Mechanical Ventilation Course Using Virtual Simulation. ATS Scholar. https://doi.org/10.34197/ats-scholar.2024-0083OC

article_title: Teacher-learner interaction quantifies scaffolding behaviour in imitation learning.
citation: Okazaki Shuntaro, Muraoka Yoshihiro, Osu Rieko. (2019). Teacher-learner interaction quantifies scaffolding behaviour in imitation learning. Scientific Reports. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-019-44049-x
title: Methodological framework quantifying scaffolding via bivariate autoregressive modelling of teacher-learner movement (Akaike causality and noise covariance)
description: The article proposes "a methodological framework for detecting the interactive scaffolding process in teaching behaviour using an imitation learning paradigm". Simultaneously recorded teacher and learner manual movements are modelled with a bivariate autoregressive model; Akaike causality quantifies bidirectional information transfer in each direction, and the model's noise covariance captures "the simultaneous component of their movement that was not explained by the bidirectional causality but identified as commonly shared driving information". Applied to a Tower of Hanoi demonstration-shadowing task, the framework maps lateral-motion influences to solution transfer and vertical-motion influences to timing monitoring.
requirements: Two distinct simultaneously recorded time series whose components can be separated to represent spatial and temporal information, as the Tower of Hanoi allows for lateral and vertical motion
constraints: The Tower of Hanoi may be difficult for infants and non-human animals; the analysis is unsuitable when demonstration and imitation occur successively and alternately rather than simultaneously; the behavioural analysis cannot discriminate instructed teaching intention from merely helping shadowing
target_learners: Adult human participants in dyadic teacher-learner pairs
target_learning_goals: Motor sequence learning by imitation; identification of scaffolding and teaching intention from behaviour
examples: Fourteen pairs performed teacher, imitation, and learner phases on a four-disk Tower of Hanoi while manual movements were recorded at 120 Hz and analysed with the framework
key_sources: Okazaki Shuntaro, Muraoka Yoshihiro, Osu Rieko. (2019). Teacher-learner interaction quantifies scaffolding behaviour in imitation learning. Scientific Reports. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-019-44049-x

article_title: Simulation Training for Residents Focused on Mechanical Ventilation: A Randomized Trial Using Mannequin-Based Versus Computer-Based Simulation.
citation: Spadaro S, Karbing DS, Fogagnolo A, Ragazzi R, Mojoli F, Astolfi L, Gioia A, Marangoni E, Rees SE, Volta CA. (2017). Simulation Training for Residents Focused on Mechanical Ventilation: A Randomized Trial Using Mannequin-Based Versus Computer-Based Simulation. Simulation in Healthcare 12(6):349-355. https://doi.org/10.1097/SIH.0000000000000249
title: Two new mechanical ventilation skill assessments: a five-scenario training assessment and an in situ high-fidelity ARDS final assessment with validity evidence
description: The authors developed two assessments for mechanical ventilation skills: a training assessment of five acute respiratory failure scenarios scored with a key action checklist and a 1–4 global rating scale, and a final assessment using in situ high-fidelity simulation of ARDS with a mannequin equipped with a lung simulator "capable of changing pulmonary resistance and compliance". Validity evidence was gathered per Kane's framework, including interrater reliability (ICC 0.87 training, 0.89 final; κ = 0.82; Cronbach α = 0.73) and regression against residency year.
requirements: Experienced instructors blinded to study group, standardized key action checklists, and video recording to support scoring validity
constraints: Pass/fail thresholds and implication validity were outside the study's scope; whether scores correlate with bedside performance requires future study
target_learning_goals: diagnosis and treatment of acute respiratory failure using appropriate mechanical ventilation settings
examples: Both groups were assessed on the same ARDS scenario in a vacant real ICU room, with a Dräger Evita XL ventilator used to avoid favoring the mannequin group
key_sources: Spadaro S, Karbing DS, Fogagnolo A, Ragazzi R, Mojoli F, Astolfi L, Gioia A, Marangoni E, Rees SE, Volta CA. (2017). Simulation Training for Residents Focused on Mechanical Ventilation: A Randomized Trial Using Mannequin-Based Versus Computer-Based Simulation. Simulation in Healthcare 12(6):349-355. https://doi.org/10.1097/SIH.0000000000000249

article_title: Effects of pre-training using serious game technology on CPR performance--an exploratory quasi-experimental transfer study.
citation: Creutzfeldt Johan, Hedman Leif, Felländer-Tsai Li. (2012). Effects of pre-training using serious game technology on CPR performance – an exploratory quasi-experimental transfer study. Scandinavian Journal of Trauma, Resuscitation and Emergency Medicine. https://doi.org/10.1186/1757-7241-20-79
title: MVW-CPR team training: a multiplayer virtual world serious game with avatars for CPR team training
description: A serious game using avatars in a multiplayer virtual world in which groups of three medical students practice team resuscitation of a collapsed cardiac-arrest victim, including examining the victim, starting resuscitation per guidelines and calling the emergency dispatcher. Training comprised a 10-minute BLS rehearsal lecture, about 20 minutes of familiarization with controlling the avatar and headset communication, four short (4–5 minute) scenarios and brief feedback sessions. The authors report it was previously found "feasible, popular and increased the subjects' concentration as well as self-efficacy beliefs".
requirements: Standard personal computers connected to the virtual world by broad band internet connections
Groups of three participants collaborating within the scenario
constraints: The authors argue the administered MVW-CPR cannot stand alone as a means of CPR training
target_learning_goals: Bystander CPR knowledge and team resuscitation skills following BLS guidelines
examples: Two sessions of MVW-CPR team training delivered 18 and 6 months before full-scale simulator assessment in this study
key_sources: Creutzfeldt Johan, Hedman Leif, Felländer-Tsai Li. (2012). Effects of pre-training using serious game technology on CPR performance – an exploratory quasi-experimental transfer study. Scandinavian Journal of Trauma, Resuscitation and Emergency Medicine. https://doi.org/10.1186/1757-7241-20-79
